children.title: Operating Systems
children.subtitle: OS Environments
children.summary: Desktop, Mobile, Server

children.title: Kernels
children.subtitle: Hardware Management
children.summary: The core program that mediates between hardware and every other layer of software.

children.title: Monolithic
children.subtitle: Single high-privileged memory space
children.summary: All operating system processes, drivers, and file systems run inside a single, high-privileged memory space. Split by how they handle code loading.

children.title: Static Monolithic
children.summary: The entire kernel and all supported hardware drivers are compiled into one unchangeable binary file. Adding a new driver or changing a core service requires recompiling the entire kernel from scratch.

children.title: Traditional UNIX (System V / Early BSD)
children.summary: The grandfather of modern operating systems. Hardware drivers, network protocols, and file systems were welded into a single block of code. Adding new hardware required manually rewriting the source code and rebuilding the entire system.

children.title: MS-DOS
children.summary: The ultimate simple monolith. It featured absolutely no separation or interior walls between user applications and the core operating system, meaning a single bug in any program would instantly crash the whole machine.

children.title: Early Linux (Pre-1995)
children.summary: The original versions of Linux. Before loadable modules were invented, if you bought a new sound card, you had to manually download its driver code, paste it into the core operating system files, and recompile the entire OS from scratch to use it.

children.title: IBM z/TPF
children.summary: A specialized ultra-fast system used by airlines and credit card networks. It runs everything in one single, raw memory space with no modular overhead, allowing it to handle millions of real-time transactions per second without slowing down.

children.title: XTS-400
children.summary: A high-assurance, military-grade operating system. It uses a rigid, unchangeable static layout so security engineers can thoroughly audit every single line of code, ensuring absolutely no hidden loopholes or modifications can be sneaked in later.

children.title: Embedded RTOS (Real-Time Operating Systems)
children.summary: The fixed software baked onto chips inside microwaves, anti-lock car brakes, or digital watches. Because these devices only perform one specific job, the kernel is permanently written at the factory, never updates, and runs instantly.

children.title: Modular Monolithic
children.summary: The system still operates in a unified, high-privileged supervisor mode, but can dynamically load or unload blocks of code — Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs) — at runtime to support new hardware or filesystems without rebooting.

children.title: Modern Linux
children.summary: Ubuntu, Debian, Red Hat — modular monolithic kernel.

children.title: FreeBSD
children.summary: A modular monolithic kernel example.

children.title: Hybrid
children.subtitle: Microkernel design, monolithic execution
children.summary: An architectural compromise that maps components like a microkernel but runs them inside a single monolithic address space to eliminate performance-slowing IPC message overhead. Split by structural composition.

children.title: Subsystem-Based Hybrids
children.summary: Isolates modular operational subsystems (like the graphics rendering manager or networking layers) inside high-privilege execution modes for maximum execution speed.

children.title: Windows NT Kernel
children.summary: Powers Windows 10 and Windows 11.

children.title: Composite / Co-Kernels
children.summary: Fuses two completely different operating system architectures directly together into a single running entity.

children.title: Apple XNU Kernel
children.summary: Powers macOS and iOS. Bridges a Mach microkernel structure together with a monolithic FreeBSD subsystem.

children.title: Microkernel
children.subtitle: Minimal core, services in user space
children.summary: The kernel is stripped down to the near-minimum code required to handle thread scheduling, virtual memory mapping, and messaging primitives. Traditional services like device drivers and file systems are kicked out into isolated user spaces. Split by design generation.

children.title: First-Generation Microkernels
children.summary: Early versions where sending data back and forth between isolated user-space processes (IPC) suffered from heavy performance overhead and slowdowns.

children.title: Early Mach
children.summary: e.g. Mach 3.0 — first-generation microkernel example.

children.title: Early Chorus
children.summary: A first-generation microkernel example.

children.title: Second-Generation Microkernels
children.summary: Redesigned from scratch to make IPC memory-page mapping fast and lightweight, with many versions formally verified for bulletproof security.

children.title: L4 Microkernel Family
children.summary: A second-generation microkernel family.

children.title: seL4
children.summary: A formally verified microkernel.

children.title: Minix 3
children.summary: A second-generation microkernel example.

children.title: QNX
children.summary: Widely deployed in automotive systems.

children.title: Nanokernel
children.subtitle: Extreme minimalism
children.summary: An extreme variation of a microkernel shrunk down to near-total minimalism, running in privileged hardware mode to offer basic hardware timing or instruction surfaces. Classified by implementation type.

children.title: HAL / Virtualization Nanokernels
children.summary: A thin software layer that handles nothing but hardware interrupt clocks and resource mapping. Often sits underneath a normal operating system to inject real-time responsiveness into it.

children.title: KeyKOS
children.summary: A HAL/virtualization nanokernel example.

children.title: Adeos
children.summary: A virtualization layer nanokernel example.

children.title: Classic PowerPC Mac OS Nanokernel
children.summary: Versions 7 through 9, handled 68k software emulation underneath.

children.title: Exokernel
children.subtitle: Protection separated from management
children.summary: An experimental paradigm that completely separates resource protection from resource management. Forces no high-level virtual abstractions (like files or directories) on developers. Defined by their reliance on application libraries.

children.title: Library Operating System (LibOS) Abstraction
children.summary: The exokernel acts strictly as a thin security guard verifying who owns a raw disk sector or memory address. Applications link directly to unprivileged libraries (Library Operating Systems) containing only the specific filesystem or network code they choose.

children.title: MIT Exokernel Projects
children.summary: XOK, Aegis — MIT exokernel research projects.

children.title: JOS
children.summary: A LibOS-abstraction exokernel example.

children.title: Nemesis
children.summary: A LibOS-abstraction exokernel example.

children.title: Unikernel
children.subtitle: App compiled with minimal system functions
children.summary: A model built upon library operating system concepts where application code is compiled directly with minimal system functions into a single, specialized, bootable binary image meant to run on a cloud hypervisor. Split by compliance standards.

children.title: Clean-Slate / Language-Specific Unikernels
children.summary: Built entirely from scratch using type-safe languages. Ignore legacy Unix standards entirely, compiling only the exact lines of code needed to make a purpose-built program execute.

children.title: MirageOS
children.summary: OCaml-based unikernel.

children.title: HaLVM
children.summary: Haskell Lightweight Virtual Machine.

children.title: LING
children.summary: Erlang-based unikernel.

children.title: Generalized / Legacy POSIX-Compliant Unikernels
children.summary: Built with backward compatibility in mind. Include a thin translation layer to simulate traditional operating system pathways, allowing standard, unmodified applications written in C, C++, or Java to compile directly into a unikernel.

children.title: OSv
children.summary: A POSIX-compliant unikernel example.

children.title: Rumprun
children.summary: Uses NetBSD rump drivers to form a unikernel footprint.

children.title: Drawbridge
children.summary: A POSIX-compliant unikernel example.
